Situation1: Your friend has misunderstood the tone of your text message and replied sounding hurt. You need to call them right now to explain.
Situation2: They scan items during a slow afternoon with a few customers in line.
Story: I stand behind the register, the soft beep of the scanner breaking the quiet of the slow afternoon. Only a few customers wait, their baskets half-full, their faces patient but expectant. My phone buzzes in my pocket, and I glance down to see a message from my friend, the words sharp and wounded. They’ve misunderstood my last text, and I can feel the urgency in their reply. I know I should call them right now, explain my tone, clear up the confusion before it festers. That’s what a good friend would do—communicate openly, resolve things before they spiral. But as a cashier, I’m expected to stay focused, process each transaction accurately, and not let personal matters interfere. My hands tremble slightly as I scan a carton of milk, my mind split between the friend who needs reassurance and the customers who expect efficiency. The weight of both roles presses on me, each demanding my full attention, and I can feel the tension building as I wrestle with what to do next.
